If you buy forestland,
 over the longer term the growth of wood will yield 5%.

Sawlog values fluctuate but wood products like poles and pilings always become scarcer and increase in value.

I pay about $350.mfbm for sawing and can do my own fall/buck/skid/load.

The mill owner picks up the logs, I haul the boards home.

In my area the annual increment is about 22 m3/ha.

At a mean value of $100/m3 each ha is growing. $ 2200 CAD/year (about half a five axle truck load)
So on my 6 ha I grow about $12,000 -$15000 value each year.

By comparison forage crops will yield about 150 small bales/ha at $6/bale or $900/ha.

Also there is an annual hay harvest in the hottest time of the year,

During haying season, I go swimming or sit in the shade. 🇨🇦

Anybody that's calling a radio show for vice on buying. Anything needs to do their own research first. For instance, if you buy vacant land and it doesn 't perk, you can't put a septic on it, and it's not able to be hooked up to city or county. Sewer, it's worthless because it's not buildable. If you can't hook up water a.k.a. city water or county water or put a well on it. It's worthless, it's not buildable, so that's literally going to be hunting. Land and that's about it. What people need to realize is when you think of property or houses or any of that stuff, it's all about location. So if you're a 100 miles from the closest store, obviously the land's not gonna be as valuable as something that's within 25 minutes. But the land also has to be buildable. So in the long and short of things you need to buy. Whatever you're going to buy, when it comes to property with a purpose, what's up? What is the purpose you're planning on doing with it? Are you planning on sitting on it and know? It's buildable, so in the future you could put your future house on it. Or sell it for a profit to a developer. Or are you buying property for hunting or farming? Or pure enjoyment of the land that is the question that meeting needs to be answered before you call in a radio show. Ramsey trusted agent. 
I contacted a half dozen near us for my daughter who just turned 18, but has worked and saved quite a bit. Was hoping to get her some professional advice so she could have a good foundation. Basically, they all said the same thing. We don’t work with people when they are first starting. Let us know when you have at least a million dollars and are nearing retirement. We’ll help you then. 

Fortunately, one did agree to a phone call to give her some tips. Might have had something to do with him being a former math teacher. 

We chose to use Fidelity as a place to put her investments, because they had local offices. We went into the office to start the process and instead of working with someone, they stuck us in a little meeting room and dialed customer service. Fortunately, that time, and on two or three occasions since, we got helped by really great customer service staff. 

It’s rather sad to hear criticism of people doing “stupid stuff” when most kids growing up are not exposed to people doing smart stuff. Even if they hear something at some point, that’s so incredibly different than having positive feedback as they are confronted with life along the way.
